title: The Construction Loan Is a Promise to Fund a Finished Building
summary: A construction loan is released in monthly draws, each one a fresh decision by the lender. Every draw rests on two checks: is the work really in place, and is there still enough money left to finish. Learn those two checks and you understand how the lender thinks for the whole build.
body:
A construction loan is not a pile of money waiting for you. It is a series of small, separate promises, each released only when the lender can see the work is in place and enough money remains to finish the building.

Recall

Q. What is an event of default in a construction loan?

A. A defined failure written into the loan agreement, such as a missed payment, a broken covenant, a false representation or insolvency, that lets the lender stop funding, demand repayment and enforce its security. Some defaults carry a notice and cure period; some do not.

Q. What is a promote in an equity waterfall?

A. The sponsor's share of profit above its share of capital, paid once investors clear agreed return hurdles. It rewards the sponsor for creating value. The splits are commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal.

Q. What does a zoning variance do?

A. It permits a departure from one specific zoning standard, such as a setback or a height limit, usually on a showing that the departure is minor or that strict compliance causes hardship. The test varies by jurisdiction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, once the first shovel goes in, you will live inside the draw cycle for two or three years. Every month you ask the lender for money, and every month the lender decides again whether to give it. A developer who understands what the lender checks gets paid on time. A developer who does not gets a delayed draw, which becomes a late payment to a subcontractor, which becomes a lien on the property, which becomes a frozen loan. That chain has stopped more good projects than bad design ever has.

This week is about the machinery of that monthly decision: the draw, the interest reserve, the lender's monitor, the in-balance test, and the guarantees and personal recourse that sit behind all of it. Today is the frame. The rest of the week fills it in.

The draw is the unit of trust

In plain English: the lender pays for the building a slice at a time, and only for the slice it can see.

The professional framing is the draw, also called an advance: one release of loan money against a package of evidence. A typical draw package holds the contractor's payment application, invoices for soft costs such as design and permits, an updated budget showing what has been spent and what remains, waivers from contractors and suppliers giving up lien rights for amounts already paid, a title update showing no new liens or charges, and a certificate signed by the borrower confirming that the representations in the loan are still true. That certificate is a statement of fact made by you. Treat it like a sworn statement, because the lender will.

The lender rarely takes your word for progress. It hires a lender's monitor: an independent engineer, cost consultant or quantity surveyor who visits the site, checks the work in place against the payment application, reviews changes and reports on whether the budget and schedule still hold. The monitor works for the lender even though the loan agreement usually makes you pay the fee. Do not mistake the monitor for your ally. The monitor is an honest witness, which is better.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. The contractor bills 1,200,000 dollars for the month. The monitor walks the site and agrees that 1,000,000 dollars of work is actually in place. The contract holds back 10 percent of each payment as retainage until completion, a commercial term in many contracts and a statutory holdback under lien law in some places; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. So the lender advances 1,000,000 dollars less 100,000 dollars of retainage, which is 900,000 dollars. The 200,000 dollars the monitor did not accept is not refused forever. It is deferred until the work exists.

The one equation: the loan must stay in balance

In plain English: at every draw, the money still available must be at least the money still needed.

The professional framing is the in-balance test. Undisbursed loan plus any equity still to be contributed must be equal to or greater than the cost to complete the project, including remaining interest, soft costs and a sensible reserve for contingency. If the sum falls short, the loan is out of balance, and the lender will not advance another dollar until you deposit the shortfall. Lenders call that deposit a balancing or rebalancing deposit. Some loans run the test in aggregate; many also run it line by line, so that savings on one budget line cannot quietly fund an overrun on another without the lender's consent. These are commercial terms, not statutory ones; your loan agreement decides which applies.

Notice the words cost to complete. Not budget remaining. Budget remaining is an accounting number: what you planned minus what you have spent. Cost to complete is a forecast: what it will really take, given what you now know. When a project is going wrong, those two numbers separate, and the in-balance test is designed to catch the moment they do.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A 20,000,000 dollar project is funded by a 14,000,000 dollar loan and 6,000,000 dollars of equity. Most lenders, as commercial practice, require the equity to be spent first, so the borrower's money is at risk before the bank's. By month 10, the equity is fully spent and the lender has advanced 6,000,000 dollars, leaving 8,000,000 dollars undisbursed. The monitor reports a cost to complete of 9,000,000 dollars because the mechanical package came in high. Eight against nine: the loan is out of balance by 1,000,000 dollars. Until you put 1,000,000 dollars into the project account, the next draw does not move, and the subcontractors waiting on it do not get paid.

Say that out loud now.

Undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover cost to complete, or I deposit the gap before the next draw.

Who pays the lender, and who stands behind the loan

Two more pieces finish the frame. First, interest. During construction there is no rent, so the loan budget usually includes an interest reserve: a line of the loan itself, set aside to pay the interest as it falls due. You are borrowing to pay the lender. On Day 3 we price it and show how a delay eats it.

Second, the backstop. Because the building is worth little until it is finished, the lender wants a person or a strong company standing behind the project. That backing comes as guarantees of completion, of cost overruns, of interest and carry, and as carve-outs that turn a limited-recourse loan into full personal liability if the borrower behaves badly. On Day 4 LEX takes you through how those documents are read and enforced.

How the best do it

The most disciplined owners do not rely on the contractor's billing or even on the lender's monitor for their picture of cost. They keep their own cost-to-complete forecast, built bottom up from the bought-out subcontracts, approved and pending changes and remaining allowances, and they reconcile it every month against the contractor's application and the monitor's report before they sign a draw certificate. Where the three numbers disagree, they find out why before the lender does. A small developer can copy this with one page: three columns, one row per budget line, and a rule that you never sign a certificate until the columns reconcile.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: how construction interest and loan fees are treated, whether added to the cost of the asset or deducted, depends on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: every draw certificate you sign is a representation, and guarantees put your own assets behind the project. Banking: a lender who receives clean, early draw packages grants waivers more readily when you need one. Governance: decide in writing who in your company may sign a draw certificate and what evidence they must see first. Estate: a personal guarantee can bind your estate after death, so your estate plan must know it exists. Exit: the construction loan is repaid only when the building is finished and refinanced or sold; staying in balance is what keeps that exit reachable.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, as borrower's counsel on the loan agreement; quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on cost to complete.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is money running ahead of work: draws approved for work that is not really in place, usually because the contractor front-loaded the early budget lines. The project then looks in balance on paper while the true cost to complete grows underneath. The control is an independent check at every draw, on quantities and not just percentages, plus your own monthly reconciliation of cost to complete against the undisbursed funds.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the loan agreement for the interest rate and the term, signs the first draw certificate without reading it, and discovers the in-balance clause in month 10, when the lender cites it to freeze funding. Read the draw conditions and the in-balance clause before you sign the commitment, and model the test monthly from day one.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage taught that contingency is not spare money but a priced estimate of what you do not yet know, and that an early-stage estimate deserves a wider range than a bought-out one. The in-balance test is where that idea gets enforced. A contingency that was too thin at the pro forma stage does not stay hidden; it shows up as an out-of-balance notice, a deposit you must make, and a lender who now watches every line.

Recap

A construction loan is released in draws, each against evidence that a lender's monitor checks. At every draw, the undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the cost to complete, or you deposit the gap. Interest is paid from a reserve inside the loan, and guarantees put real people behind the finished building.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of an overpaid contractor and a called guarantee.
checklist: I have read the draw conditions and the in-balance clause before signing the commitment.
I know who the lender's monitor is and what each monthly report covers.
I keep my own cost-to-complete forecast, line by line.
I reconcile billing, the monitor's report and my forecast before signing any draw certificate.
I know whether my loan tests balance in aggregate, line by line, or both.
I know how much equity must go in first and when it is fully spent.
I have decided in writing who may sign a draw certificate.
My estate plan records every guarantee I have signed.
head: Field checklist
speak: A construction loan is not a pile of money. It is a series of monthly releases called draws. Each draw rests on two checks. First, is the work really in place? The lender's monitor, an independent engineer or cost consultant, walks the site and agrees or disagrees with the contractor's bill. Second, is there still enough money to finish? That is the in-balance test: the undisbursed loan plus any equity still to come must cover the cost to complete. If it does not, I deposit the shortfall before the lender advances another dollar. Cost to complete is a forecast, not budget remaining, and that difference is where projects fail. Interest is paid from a reserve inside the loan, and guarantees put real people behind the finished building. So I keep my own cost-to-complete forecast and reconcile it every month before I sign a draw certificate, because that certificate is a statement of fact.
terms: Draw — one release of construction loan money, made against a package of evidence that the work is in place.
Lender's monitor — an independent engineer, cost consultant or quantity surveyor hired to verify progress and cost on the lender's behalf.
In-balance test — the requirement that undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity covers the full cost to complete before any further draw.

hostile.q: Your monitor says cost to complete exceeds the undisbursed funds by 1,000,000 dollars. Why should I fund this month's draw?
hostile.a: You should not, and I am not asking you to until the gap is closed. I will deposit the shortfall into the project account, or show you committed equity that covers it, before the draw moves. I also want to walk you through where the overrun came from, what we have done to stop it growing, and the revised cost-to-complete forecast line by line, so you can test it against your monitor's numbers.

title: The Overpaid Contractor and the Called Guarantee
summary: A composite case: a contractor billed ahead of the work, the draws followed the billing, and the contractor failed with the job half built. The true cost to complete then exceeded the money left, and the lender called the developer's personal guarantees. Seven forensic steps show where it could have been stopped.
body:
This is a composite example. A contractor billed ahead of the work, the draws followed the bills, and when the contractor failed, the gap between money left and cost to complete landed on the developer personally.

Recall

Q. What does the in-balance test require?

A. That the undisbursed loan plus any equity still to come covers the full cost to complete. If not, the borrower deposits the shortfall before the next draw.

Q. In an equity waterfall, what is a clawback?

A. An obligation on the sponsor to return promote it received early if, at the end of the deal, investors did not actually achieve the agreed return. It is a negotiated term, not a default rule.

Q. What is a development agreement in the entitlement process?

A. A contract between a developer and a public authority setting out what the developer will build or pay for, such as roads, utilities or contributions, in exchange for approvals. Its form and enforceability depend on local law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me today because this failure is told in two currencies: the money that went out of the loan too early, and the personal liability that came back in through the guarantees. No single fact in this story is exotic. That is the point. Every step was a normal, defensible decision at the time, and together they carried a developer from a healthy project to a personal claim against his own assets.

This is a composite example, assembled from patterns that recur in construction lending. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

1. Timeline

A developer begins a 30,000,000 dollar mid-rise residential building, funded by a 21,000,000 dollar construction loan and 9,000,000 dollars of equity, spent first. He signs a completion guarantee and a cost-overrun guarantee in his own name. In month 2, the contractor submits its schedule of values: the list of budget lines it will bill against. Mobilisation, general conditions and site work are priced high. In month 2, the lender's monitor notes that the early lines look heavy. By month 9, the contractor has billed 55 percent of the contract. In month 11 the contractor stops paying subcontractors, liens appear on title, and the contractor enters insolvency. A replacement contractor prices the remaining work. Cost to complete now exceeds undisbursed funds by 4,000,000 dollars. The lender declares the loan out of balance, the developer cannot fund the gap, and the lender calls the guarantees.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Accepting a contractor with thin balance sheet strength because its price was lowest. Accepting a front-loaded schedule of values to keep the start date. And continuing to sign monthly draw certificates stating the loan was in balance, on the strength of budget remaining rather than an independent cost-to-complete forecast.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed that because the monitor approved each draw, the money was matched to the work. But the monitor was checking percentages of budget lines, and a percentage of an inflated line is still inflated. He assumed that retainage would cover any problem with the contractor. Retainage was 10 percent of what had been paid; the overbilling plus the cost of re-procuring the work was far larger. He assumed the guarantee he signed was a formality that lenders never enforce.

4. Incentives

The contractor had every incentive to bill early: cash in hand protects a contractor with weak working capital. The developer had an incentive to keep draws moving, because a delayed draw angers subcontractors and slows the job. The lender's monitor was paid to report, not to stop the project, and its scope was narrower than the developer believed. Each incentive was rational. None of them protected the cost to complete.

Say that out loud now.

Every party was rational. Nobody was paid to protect the cost to complete except me.

5. Warning signs ignored

The monitor's month-2 note on heavy early lines. A contractor billing 55 percent complete on a job the developer's own eyes would have put near 40 percent. Subcontractor complaints of slow payment, which arrived in month 7. A request from the contractor to reduce retainage early. Each of these is a classic signal that cash is moving ahead of work or that the contractor is short of cash.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was month 9, the last draw before the failure. Up to then, the developer could have stopped paying ahead, rebalanced the schedule of values, demanded a performance bond claim or replaced the contractor while the overbilling was still small. After that draw, the cash was gone into an insolvent company, and the only remaining question was who would fund the hole.

Notice what was still available at month 8. A performance bond, if the contract had required one, would have given the developer a surety to call, with its own obligation to complete or pay. A payment bond would have protected subcontractors and reduced the liens. A tighter retainage clause would have held more cash back. None of these is free, and each is a commercial term to price at award. But each moves part of the contractor's failure onto someone whose business is carrying it, rather than onto the developer's personal guarantee. Week 79 covers surety in depth.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not the insolvency. Contractors fail. The root cause was that the owner let the draw process measure billing rather than work in place, and certified balance on budget remaining rather than on an independent cost to complete. That turned an ordinary contractor failure into a funding gap, and the funding gap into a personal claim.

Roman's view: how the guarantees bit

Here is the lender's arithmetic, hypothetical. The out-of-balance amount was 4,000,000 dollars. Under the cost-overrun guarantee, the developer had promised to pay costs above budget. Under the completion guarantee, he had promised to deliver the building lien-free. The lender's first demand was for the 4,000,000 dollars. Had the project stalled long enough for the lender to enforce, the loss could have been larger: a half-built building sells at a deep discount, and a completion guarantee can expose the guarantor to the cost of finishing, not only the overrun. Read Day 4 for how courts read these documents. The lesson for today is simpler: a personal guarantee converts an operational failure into your personal balance sheet.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that draws track billing instead of work in place, so the loan looks in balance until the day the contractor stops. The control is a schedule of values reviewed line by line before the first draw, a monitor scope that verifies quantities, and an owner's own cost-to-complete forecast reconciled every month.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the monitor's approval as his protection. It is the lender's protection, and its scope is whatever the lender bought. The second beginner's mistake is choosing the lowest price without asking whether the contractor can survive a bad month: check its finances, its bonding and its payment record with subcontractors.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and ask why. Run that drill on any construction loan and the first answer is almost always the contractor, and the second is cash moving ahead of work. The developer in this case could have written his own failure story on day one. He would have found the month-2 note on the schedule of values sitting in the first paragraph.

Recap

Draws followed billing, billing ran ahead of work, the contractor failed, cost to complete exceeded funds, and the guarantees moved the gap onto the developer personally. The prevention is to make every draw prove work in place and to certify balance only on an independent cost to complete.

Rule 40: Never let a draw run ahead of verified work in place, and never certify the loan in balance on budget remaining; certify it only on an independent cost to complete.

Next: Priya on The Money: what the interest reserve and the guarantees cost, and how they move your returns.
checklist: I review the contractor's schedule of values line by line before the first draw.
I compare billed percentage with my own estimate of work in place every month.
I confirm the monitor's scope covers quantities, not only percentages.
I check the contractor's finances, bonding and subcontractor payment record before award.
I treat slow subcontractor payment as an early warning, not gossip.
I refuse early reductions in retainage while work is unfinished.
I certify balance only on an independent cost to complete.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A developer took the lowest-priced contractor and accepted a front-loaded schedule of values to keep the start date. The monitor noted heavy early lines in month 2, but the draws kept following the bills. By month 9 the contractor had billed 55 percent on a job closer to 40 percent complete. In month 11 it failed. The replacement price showed a 4,000,000 dollar gap between cost to complete and the money left. The loan went out of balance, and the lender called the developer's completion and cost-overrun guarantees. The root cause was not the insolvency; contractors fail. It was letting draws measure billing instead of work in place, and certifying balance on budget remaining. Rule 40: never let a draw run ahead of verified work in place, and certify balance only on an independent cost to complete.
terms: Schedule of values — the contractor's list of budget lines and amounts that each payment application is billed against.
Front-loading — pricing early schedule lines high so the contractor collects cash ahead of the value of work done.
Cost-overrun guarantee — a promise by a guarantor to pay project costs that exceed the approved budget.

hostile.q: Your contractor failed and the loan is out of balance by 4,000,000 dollars. Your guarantee covers it. When do I get the money?
hostile.a: I will give you a written plan within a set number of days, not a promise today. It will show the replacement contractor's priced cost to complete, the sources that close the gap, including any bond or retainage recoveries from the failed contractor, and the date each source lands. I am not disputing the guarantee. I am asking you to judge my plan against the cost of you enforcing on a half-built building.

rule: Rule 40: Never let a draw run ahead of verified work in place, and never certify the loan in balance on budget remaining; certify it only on an independent cost to complete.

title: What the Interest Reserve and the Guarantees Really Cost
summary: The interest reserve is borrowed money that pays the lender, so it raises cost and lowers yield on cost. A delay drains it fast because the loan is nearly fully drawn by then. Guarantees cost nothing on day one and can cost everything later, which is why they belong on your personal balance sheet.
body:
The interest reserve is money you borrow to pay the lender, and every month of delay spends it at the highest rate the project will ever pay. Guarantees cost nothing on the day you sign them and can cost everything later.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between budget remaining and cost to complete?

A. Budget remaining is the plan less what has been spent, an accounting number. Cost to complete is a forecast of what finishing will really take, given what is now known. The in-balance test uses cost to complete.

Q. What is a preferred return?

A. A priority return to investors on contributed capital, paid before the sponsor shares in profit. Whether it compounds and whether it is cumulative are negotiated terms.

Q. In entitlements, what is a condition of approval?

A. A requirement attached to a planning approval, such as a road improvement, a contribution or a design change, that the developer must meet. Conditions carry cost and time and belong in the pro forma.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, two lines in your budget behave unlike any others. The interest reserve grows with every month of delay and every rate rise, and it is itself borrowed, so it carries interest on interest. The guarantee line is not in the budget at all, yet it is the largest contingent cost you carry. A developer who prices both properly negotiates a better loan and sleeps better during the build.

Sizing the interest reserve

In plain English: interest during construction is paid on the money actually drawn, and the loan is drawn gradually, so the average balance is well below the full loan.

The professional framing: construction spending follows an S-curve, slow at the start, fast in the middle, slow at the end. The average outstanding balance over the build is commonly modelled at roughly half to 60 percent of the commitment, though the real figure depends on how much equity goes in first and the shape of your schedule. After completion, during lease-up, the loan is close to fully drawn and there is little rent yet, so those months cost the most.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A 14,000,000 dollar loan at 8 percent a year, 18 months of construction, then 6 months of lease-up. Construction interest: 14,000,000 times 0.55 average utilisation times 0.08 times 1.5 years is about 924,000 dollars. Lease-up interest: assume the loan is fully drawn and rent covers about half the interest, so the reserve must fund the other half. 14,000,000 times 0.08 times 0.5 years is 560,000 dollars, and half of that is 280,000 dollars. The reserve is about 1,204,000 dollars before one more adjustment.

That adjustment is the gross-up. The reserve is drawn from the loan, so the reserve itself accrues interest. On a reserve of about 1,200,000 dollars drawn steadily over two years, that adds tens of thousands of dollars. Most models handle it with an iterative calculation. The habit to keep: never size the reserve once and leave it; recalculate it whenever the schedule or the rate moves.

The other finance costs that ride on every draw

The reserve is the largest finance cost, but not the only one. As commercial practice, a construction loan usually carries an upfront fee on the commitment, sometimes a fee on unused commitment, the lender's legal fees, the monitor's monthly fee, and a title update charge for each draw. Each is small alone. Together, on a two-year build, they can approach the size of a month or two of interest. Put each one on its own budget line with its own trigger, so that a longer schedule automatically raises the monitor and title costs in your model. A schedule slip does not only add interest; it adds a monthly invoice from everyone the lender requires you to pay.

Say that out loud now.

The reserve is borrowed, so delay costs me interest on the interest, at the loan's highest balance.

What a delay does to the numbers

Worked example two, continuing. Construction runs 4 months late. In those 4 months the loan is nearly fully drawn, say 13,000,000 dollars outstanding. Extra interest is 13,000,000 times 0.08 times 4 divided by 12, about 347,000 dollars. That money must come from somewhere. If the reserve has no cushion, it comes from contingency. If contingency is already committed, the loan goes out of balance and you deposit the gap.

Now see the effect on value. Suppose the project was planned at a total cost of 20,000,000 dollars and a stabilised net operating income (NOI), meaning rent less operating expenses, of 1,400,000 dollars. Yield on cost was 1,400,000 divided by 20,000,000, which is 7.0 percent. Add 347,000 dollars of delay interest and cost becomes about 20,347,000 dollars. Yield on cost falls to about 6.88 percent. On a project whose development spread over market cap rates was planned at 1.5 percentage points, you have just spent about an eighth of your margin on time alone, before any construction overrun. Your levered internal rate of return (IRR) falls further, because the equity is tied up 4 months longer and the profit is smaller.

The cost of the guarantees

Guarantees have three costs. The first is visible: some guarantors charge a fee to the project for providing them, which, as commercial practice, may be negotiated with partners and has its own tax character to verify. The second is the liquidity the lender makes you keep. Many guarantees come with covenants that the guarantor maintain a minimum net worth and a minimum of liquid assets throughout the loan, a commercial term. That cash is not free to invest elsewhere. The third is the expected loss: the chance the guarantee is called, times what it would cost. It is small on a well-run project and large on a badly run one, which is why your control systems are the cheapest way to reduce it.

Lenders also price the guarantee into the loan. A strong, liquid completion guarantor can earn better pricing, a higher loan-to-cost, or fewer conditions. A weak one costs you in those terms. You are, in effect, selling the lender a piece of your personal balance sheet in exchange for cheaper money.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, a guarantee is a contingent liability: a debt that exists only if something goes wrong. Accounting rules for a person's own statement are informal, so record it yourself, on a separate line, at the full amount you could be asked to pay and with a note of the probability you assign to it. Then check two things. First, does your liquidity floor, the cash you never touch, survive a call on your largest guarantee? Second, how much of your net worth is promised to a single project? Concentration hides inside guarantees, because the asset is in one column and the promise sits off the page. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of this for your own affairs.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an interest reserve sized on the original schedule and never revisited, so that a delay quietly converts into an out-of-balance demand at the worst possible time. The control is to re-run the reserve every month against the current schedule and the current rate, and to carry a stated cushion for delay inside it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the guarantee as free because it costs nothing at closing. It costs liquidity you must hold, terms you could have negotiated, and a probability of loss that depends entirely on how well you run the job.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage warned that IRR is sensitive to time as much as to profit: the same dollar of profit earned later is worth less. A construction delay is that warning made concrete. It shrinks the profit through interest and stretches the time the equity is tied up, so it attacks IRR from both sides at once.

Recap

Size the interest reserve on an S-curve for construction and near full balance for lease-up, gross it up because it is borrowed, and re-run it whenever the schedule or rate moves. Delay costs interest at the loan's highest balance and eats yield on cost. Guarantees cost liquidity, terms and expected loss; record them on your personal balance sheet as contingent liabilities.

Next: LEX on The Rules: how guarantees and carve-outs are written, read and enforced.
checklist: I size the interest reserve on a monthly draw curve, not a single average.
I include lease-up months at close to full loan balance.
I gross up the reserve because it is itself borrowed.
I re-run the reserve whenever the schedule or the rate moves.
I know the extra interest cost of one month of delay.
I know the net worth and liquidity covenants attached to my guarantees.
I record every guarantee as a contingent liability on my personal balance sheet.

speak: The interest reserve is a line of the loan set aside to pay interest during construction. I size it on the draw curve: the average balance during construction is often around half to 60 percent of the loan, while lease-up months run at nearly full balance with little rent. Because the reserve is borrowed, it carries interest on itself, so I gross it up and re-run it whenever the schedule or rate changes. A four-month delay on a 13,000,000 dollar balance at 8 percent costs about 347,000 dollars, which can drop yield on cost from 7.0 to about 6.88 percent and push the loan out of balance. Guarantees cost nothing at closing, but they cost liquidity I must hold, terms I trade, and an expected loss that depends on how well I run the job. On my own balance sheet, every guarantee is a contingent liability, recorded at full amount.
terms: Interest reserve — a budgeted portion of the construction loan set aside to pay interest as it falls due before the project earns income.
Gross-up — increasing a borrowed reserve to cover the interest that accrues on the reserve itself.
Contingent liability — an obligation that becomes payable only if a future event occurs, such as a guarantee being called.

hostile.q: Your interest reserve assumes 18 months. What happens to this loan if you are six months late?
hostile.a: I have modelled it. Six months at close to full balance costs roughly the loan balance times the rate times half a year, which on these numbers is around 520,000 dollars. The reserve carries a stated delay cushion of part of that, contingency carries the rest, and if both are used I will make a balancing deposit from committed equity that I can show you today. I would rather agree that trigger now than argue about it in month 20.

title: Guarantees and Carve-Outs: How the Promise Is Read
summary: A guarantee is a written promise to answer for someone else's obligation, and the law reads it strictly. Completion, cost-overrun, carry and repayment guarantees cover different risks, while carve-outs turn a limited-recourse loan into personal liability on defined bad acts. Read every trigger, cap and waiver before you sign.
body:
A guarantee is a promise to answer for someone else's debt, and courts read it by its words. What you guarantee, when it can be called and what defences you have given away are all decided in drafting, not later.

Recall

Q. Why does a delay cost so much interest?

A. Because by the time a project is late, the loan is nearly fully drawn, so each extra month is charged on close to the full balance, and the interest reserve that pays it is itself borrowed.

Q. What is a commitment letter in construction lending?

A. The lender's written offer to make the loan on stated terms, usually subject to conditions precedent and to final loan documents. What binds, and when, depends on its wording.

Q. What is the difference between a promote and a developer fee?

A. A developer fee is paid for services, usually from the budget, whether or not the deal makes money. A promote is a share of profit paid only if investors clear their hurdles. Their tax character often differs; verify that against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, your loan may be called limited recourse or non-recourse, but the guarantees decide what that phrase actually means for you. Two developers can sign loans with the same rate and the same amount and carry very different personal exposure, because one negotiated caps, burn-offs and narrow triggers, and the other signed the lender's first draft. This lesson teaches concepts and how to read the documents. It does not decide any question under a particular jurisdiction's law.

What a guarantee is in law

In plain English: a guarantee is your promise that if the borrower does not perform, you will.

The professional framing, in common-law systems generally, separates two things. A guarantee is a secondary obligation: you answer for the borrower's obligation, so your liability usually rises and falls with it. An indemnity is a primary obligation: you promise to make the lender whole for a loss, whether or not the borrower is liable. Lenders often draft guarantees to work as both, using phrases such as "as principal obligor and not merely as surety", so that defences that would protect a pure guarantor do not apply. Many common-law jurisdictions also require a guarantee to be in writing and signed to be enforceable. Verify both points against the primary source before you rely on them.

A second principle runs through the case law of many common-law systems: a guarantor can be released if the creditor and the borrower materially change the guaranteed obligation without the guarantor's consent, because the guarantor did not agree to the new risk. Lenders know this, so their guarantees contain waivers in which you consent in advance to amendments, extensions and releases of security. When you sign those waivers, you give up a protection the law would otherwise give you. Read them with your eyes open.

The four main guarantees in a construction loan

A completion guarantee promises that the project will be finished, lien-free, according to the approved plans, within a stated time. It can expose the guarantor to the full cost of finishing, and in some drafts to the lender's losses if it is not finished.

A cost-overrun guarantee promises to pay costs above the approved budget. The important questions are what counts as an overrun, whether contingency must be exhausted first, and whether it is capped.

A carry guarantee, sometimes called an interest and operating deficit guarantee, promises to pay interest, taxes, insurance and operating shortfalls until the property reaches a defined stabilisation test.

A repayment guarantee, sometimes called a payment guarantee, promises to repay principal, in full or up to a cap or percentage. A loan with a full repayment guarantee is full recourse in substance, whatever it is called.

Say that out loud now.

Completion, overrun, carry, repayment: four different promises, four different triggers, four different caps.

Carve-outs: when limited recourse stops being limited

A loan described as non-recourse or limited recourse usually carries a carve-out guarantee, sometimes called a bad-acts guarantee. It names events that switch personal liability back on. Commercial practice divides them in two. Loss carve-outs make the guarantor liable for the lender's actual loss from the act, for example misapplying rents or insurance money, fraud, physical waste, or failing to pay taxes from available cash. Full-recourse carve-outs, often called springing recourse, make the guarantor liable for the whole debt on events such as a voluntary bankruptcy filing by the borrower, or a transfer or further charge on the property without consent. An environmental indemnity is frequently a separate document, and it may survive repayment of the loan.

The drafting war is over vagueness. A carve-out triggered by "any breach of the separateness covenants" can catch a clerical slip. A carve-out for failing to pay taxes can be limited to taxes the borrower had cash to pay. Narrow, objective, within your control: that is what you negotiate for.

Two clauses read side by side

Worked example one, hypothetical. Clause A: "Guarantor guarantees payment of all Project Costs in excess of the Budget." Clause B: "Guarantor guarantees payment of Project Costs in excess of the Budget, after application of the unallocated contingency, up to a maximum of 2,000,000 dollars, such obligation terminating on Completion." Clause A is uncapped, ignores contingency and never ends. Clause B uses contingency first, caps exposure and burns off at completion. On a project with a 3,000,000 dollar overrun and 1,000,000 dollars of contingency, Clause A exposes you to 3,000,000 dollars and Clause B to 2,000,000 dollars, with nothing owed after completion. Note that "Completion" must itself be defined objectively, for example by an occupancy certificate and the monitor's confirmation, or it can be argued about for years.

Two more drafting points decide how a guarantee behaves when it is called. First, demand: some guarantees are payable on the lender's written demand, without the lender first pursuing the borrower or selling the property; others require the lender to exhaust its remedies first. Lenders prefer the first, and most institutional drafts say so. Second, continuity: a continuing guarantee covers the borrower's obligations as they change over time, including new advances and extensions, until it is formally released. If you sell your interest in the project and leave the deal, a continuing guarantee does not end because you left. You must negotiate and obtain a written release, usually in exchange for a replacement guarantor the lender accepts.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A carry guarantee ends "upon Stabilisation", defined as a debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), which is NOI divided by debt service, of 1.25 for two consecutive quarters. If rents lag and the ratio sits at 1.20, you keep paying shortfalls indefinitely. A negotiated version adds an outside date, after which the obligation ends, or converts to a cap. The ratio is a commercial term, not a standard.

Independent advice and the household

Lenders commonly require that a guarantor receive independent legal advice and sometimes ask for a spouse's guarantee or consent where assets are jointly held. That is commercial practice and, in some places, a response to case law on guarantees signed under pressure. Your own counsel should advise you, not the lender's.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, acting for you as guarantor, separate from the borrower's and lender's counsel.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an uncapped, never-ending guarantee with broad springing triggers, signed because the lender called it standard. The control is to negotiate four things on every guarantee: a cap, a burn-off date, objective triggers within your control, and a defined completion or stabilisation test with an outside date.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the loan agreement closely and skims the guarantee because it is short. The guarantee is the document that reaches your house. Read it first.

Callback

In Week 21, LEX and Omar taught that limited liability protects the shareholder unless the company is used improperly, and that courts can pierce the corporate veil. A personal guarantee is the voluntary version: you lift the veil yourself, in writing, for a price. Carve-outs are the lender's way of making sure that improper use of the company lifts it automatically.

Recap

A guarantee is secondary, an indemnity is primary, and lenders draft to get both. Completion, cost-overrun, carry and repayment guarantees cover different risks. Carve-outs convert limited recourse into loss or full recourse on defined acts. Negotiate caps, burn-offs, objective triggers and defined tests, and take independent advice.

Next: Priya on The Numbers: reverse engineering an out-of-balance notice back to its causes.
checklist: I read the guarantee before the loan agreement.
I know whether each guarantee is capped, and at what amount.
I know the burn-off date or event for each guarantee.
I know which carve-outs trigger loss recourse and which trigger full recourse.
Completion and stabilisation are defined by objective tests with an outside date.
I understand which legal defences my waivers give up.
I take advice from my own lawyer, not the lender's.
I know whether the environmental indemnity survives repayment.
head: Field checklist
speak: A guarantee is my promise to perform if the borrower does not. In common-law systems a guarantee is usually secondary, rising and falling with the borrower's debt, while an indemnity is primary; lenders draft to get both, and their waivers remove defences the law would otherwise give me. A construction loan carries four main guarantees: completion, cost overrun, carry until stabilisation, and repayment of principal. Carve-outs turn a limited-recourse loan back into personal liability on defined bad acts, some for the lender's actual loss, some springing to the full debt. I negotiate four things on every guarantee: a cap, a burn-off, objective triggers within my control, and a defined completion or stabilisation test with an outside date. I read the guarantee first, because it is the document that reaches my house, and I take advice from my own lawyer.
terms: Indemnity — a primary promise to make someone whole for a loss, owed whether or not another party is liable.
Carve-out guarantee — a guarantee that switches personal liability on for defined bad acts under an otherwise limited-recourse loan.
Burn-off — the date or event at which a guarantee ends or steps down.

hostile.q: Every borrower signs our standard full-recourse completion guarantee. Why should we cap yours?
hostile.a: Because the risk you are pricing is construction risk, and it reduces sharply at defined points. I will give you completion with contingency applied first, a cap sized to a realistic overrun, and a burn-off at completion defined by the occupancy certificate and your monitor's sign-off. In exchange I will accept tighter draw controls and monthly cost-to-complete reporting, which protect you more than an uncapped promise from someone you would rather not sue.

title: Reverse Engineering an Out-of-Balance Notice
summary: Start from a finished outcome, an out-of-balance notice and an exhausted interest reserve, and work backward to the causes. The method separates what came from overruns, what came from delay and what came from rate. Each answer points to a different control.
body:
An out-of-balance notice is a total. Work it backward and it splits into three causes, overrun, delay and rate, and each cause tells you which control failed.

Recall

Q. What is a springing recourse carve-out?

A. A carve-out that makes the guarantor liable for the whole loan, not just the lender's loss, on defined events such as a voluntary bankruptcy filing or an unauthorised transfer. It is commercial practice and varies by loan.

Q. What is a catch-up in an equity waterfall?

A. A tier that, after investors receive their preferred return, sends a large share of cash to the sponsor until the sponsor has received its agreed share of total profit to that point.

Q. What is a pre-application meeting in entitlements?

A. An early meeting with planning staff, before a formal application, to learn the issues they will raise and the studies they will require, reducing redesign and delay later.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender will one day send you a number: the loan is out of balance by a stated amount. If you can split that number into its causes the same afternoon, you control the conversation, you fix the right thing, and you know which guarantee is in play. Today we reverse engineer: start from a finished outcome and work backward. All numbers are hypothetical.

The finished outcome

Here is what the lender sends in month 20. Project budget at closing: 20,000,000 dollars. Loan: 14,000,000 dollars at a planned 8 percent. Equity: 6,000,000 dollars, spent first, now fully spent. Budgeted interest reserve: 1,200,000 dollars for 18 months of construction and 6 months of lease-up. Today, the lender has advanced 12,600,000 dollars, of which 1,200,000 dollars was interest, so the reserve is exhausted. Undisbursed loan: 1,400,000 dollars. The monitor's cost to complete, including interest to stabilisation: 2,900,000 dollars. The notice reads: out of balance by 1,500,000 dollars, being 2,900,000 less 1,400,000.

We want three answers: how much of that 1,500,000 dollars is construction overrun, how much is delay, and how much is rate.

Step 1: reverse out the delay

The monitor's schedule shows completion in month 22 instead of month 18: a 4-month delay. Over those months the loan balance averaged about 12,000,000 dollars. The rate is floating and has averaged 9 percent instead of the planned 8.

Delay interest at the planned rate: 12,000,000 dollars times 0.08 times 4 divided by 12 equals 320,000 dollars.

Units check: dollars times a rate per year times years gives dollars. Good.

Step 2: reverse out the rate

The extra 1 percentage point applies to the whole time the loan was outstanding, not only the delay. Estimate the average balance over the 20 months to date at about 7,000,000 dollars. Rate effect to date: 7,000,000 times 0.01 times 20 divided by 12 equals about 117,000 dollars. The extra point also applies to the delay months: 12,000,000 times 0.01 times 4 divided by 12 equals 40,000 dollars. Total rate effect: about 157,000 dollars.

That explains why the reserve ran out early. It was spent faster because each month cost more.

Say that out loud now.

Delay, rate, overrun: I split the gap into three before I answer the lender.

Step 3: the remainder is construction overrun

Out of balance: 1,500,000 dollars. Less delay interest: 320,000 dollars. Less rate effect: 157,000 dollars. Remainder: 1,023,000 dollars. That is the construction and soft-cost overrun, after contingency was used. The monitor's report should confirm it line by line, for example a curtain wall package that bought out above its allowance and design fees for changes.

Now the three causes are visible: about 1,023,000 dollars of overrun, about 320,000 dollars of delay and about 157,000 dollars of rate. Rounding in the averages means your figures will not tie to the dollar; reconcile them to the monitor's figures before you present them.

Step 4: map each cause to a control and a guarantee

The overrun points to buyout and change control: the packages that came in high, and whether changes were priced before they were approved. It is the cost-overrun guarantee's territory.

The delay points to the schedule: the critical path, the procurement of long-lead items, and the contractor's resources. It may be the contractor's liability under its contract, through liquidated damages if the contract provides them, which is a recovery source to pursue.

The rate points to the financing decision: a floating rate without a hedge or cap. That was a choice made at closing, and the lesson is to price it next time. It falls under the carry guarantee once the project is complete.

A second worked example: how big was the reserve meant to be?

Reverse engineer the reserve itself. Suppose the project had finished on time at the planned rate. Construction interest on a 14,000,000 dollar loan averaging 55 percent drawn over 18 months at 8 percent is about 924,000 dollars. Lease-up of 6 months at full balance is 560,000 dollars; if rent covers half, the reserve funds 280,000 dollars. Total about 1,204,000 dollars, which matches the 1,200,000 dollar budget. So the reserve was sized correctly for the plan, with no cushion. The defect was not the arithmetic; it was the absence of a delay and rate allowance. A reserve with a cushion of, say, 4 months of interest at full balance, about 373,000 dollars at 8 percent, would have absorbed the delay and left the overrun as the real conversation.

A third check: in balance overall, out of balance by line

Now run the test the way many loan agreements also run it: line by line. Suppose, in a different month, the aggregate test passes. Undisbursed funds are 3,000,000 dollars; total cost to complete is 2,900,000 dollars. Good. But the line-by-line view shows the mechanical line needs 1,300,000 dollars against 1,000,000 dollars remaining, while the landscaping line shows 400,000 dollars remaining against 100,000 dollars needed.

Work it backward. The aggregate cushion of 100,000 dollars exists only because the landscaping saving of 300,000 dollars covers the mechanical overrun of 300,000 dollars. Under a line-by-line clause, you may not move that saving without the lender's consent, and some agreements allow reallocation only after the saving line is complete and the saving is real. So the honest position is: in balance overall, out of balance on mechanical by 300,000 dollars, pending a reallocation request.

The habit: when you submit a reallocation, show that the donor line's saving is earned, not hoped for. A saving on landscaping that has not yet been bought out is an estimate. A lender's monitor will say so, and you will have spent credibility asking.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is answering the lender with a single number. A single number invites a single remedy, usually your money. The control is to bring the split: overrun, delay and rate, each with its source, its recovery route and the guarantee it touches.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on the overrun reconciliation; lawyer, before you tell the lender which guarantee a cause falls under, because that statement can be used against you later. Your split is a working analysis for the conversation, not an admission, and your counsel should see it before it leaves your desk.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner adds the delay months but forgets that a floating rate applied to every month the loan was outstanding. Rate effects are small per month and large in total, and they drain the reserve before anyone notices.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal from public information: start with the answer and solve for the inputs. The same move works on your own project. The out-of-balance notice is the answer; overrun, delay and rate are the inputs; and once you have solved for them, you know what to fix and what to recover.

Recap

Start from the notice, reverse out delay interest at the planned rate, then the rate effect over the whole loan, and treat the remainder as overrun. Map each to its control and its guarantee. Size the next reserve with an explicit cushion for delay and rate.

Next: Roman on The Room: the draw meeting where the monitor reports an overrun.
checklist: I can split any out-of-balance amount into overrun, delay and rate.
I check units on every interest calculation.
I apply a rate change to every month the loan was outstanding.
I reconcile my split to the monitor's line-by-line report.
I identify recovery sources such as liquidated damages before I offer my own money.
I size the interest reserve with an explicit cushion for delay and rate.
I know which guarantee each cause touches.
head: Field checklist
speak: When the lender says the loan is out of balance, I work the number backward. In this hypothetical, the gap is 1,500,000 dollars: cost to complete of 2,900,000 against 1,400,000 undisbursed. First I reverse out delay: four extra months on about 12,000,000 dollars at the planned 8 percent is about 320,000 dollars. Then rate: the floating rate averaged one point higher across the whole loan, about 157,000 dollars. The remainder, about 1,023,000 dollars, is construction overrun after contingency. Each cause has its own control and its own guarantee. Overrun points to buyout and change control. Delay points to the schedule and possibly liquidated damages from the contractor. Rate points to an unhedged choice made at closing. I bring the lender the split, not a single number, and I size the next reserve with an explicit cushion for delay and rate.
terms: Rebalancing deposit — cash the borrower puts into the project to cure an out-of-balance loan before further draws.
Floating rate — an interest rate that resets periodically with a reference rate, so the cost of borrowing changes during the loan.
Liquidated damages — a contractually agreed amount payable for a defined breach, such as late completion.

hostile.q: You say only 1,023,000 dollars is overrun. Why should I accept your split instead of treating the whole 1,500,000 dollars as your cost overrun?
hostile.a: You do not have to accept it on my word. Here is the reconciliation to your monitor's line items for the overrun, the schedule showing the four-month slip, and the rate history from your own statements. The split matters to both of us: the delay may be recoverable from the contractor, and the rate effect continues every month we stay unhedged. I will fund the gap either way. The split tells us how to stop it growing.

title: The Draw Meeting When the Monitor Reports an Overrun
summary: A monthly draw meeting where the lender's monitor reports that cost to complete has passed the undisbursed funds. The scene gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the lender's question, and when to stay silent. The goal is to leave with trust intact and a dated plan.
body:
When the monitor reports an overrun, the lender is not asking whether you are sorry. The lender is asking whether you still have control of the project, and every sentence you say is evidence for or against.

Recall

Q. How do you reverse engineer an out-of-balance notice?

A. Reverse out delay interest at the planned rate, then the rate effect over every month the loan was outstanding, and treat the remainder as construction overrun, reconciled to the monitor's line items.

Q. What is a developer fee and when is it usually paid?

A. A fee for development services, usually paid from the project budget in instalments during the build. Lenders often defer part of it until completion as commercial practice.

Q. What is an appeal in the entitlement process?

A. A challenge to a planning decision before a tribunal or court, brought by the applicant or by objectors. It adds time and uncertainty, which belong in the schedule and the pro forma.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, I sit on the lender's side of this table, so I will tell you what I am listening for. I have seen developers lose a lender's confidence not because of the overrun but because of how they handled the meeting. A loan agreement gives the lender wide discretion on waivers, consents and the speed of draws. That discretion follows trust, and trust is built or spent in rooms like this one.

The scene

Month 14 of an 18-month build. Around the table: the lender's relationship manager, the lender's construction risk officer, the lender's monitor, and you. Your contractor's project manager waits outside, available if called. The monitor presents. Cost to complete has risen by 1,100,000 dollars since last month, driven by the mechanical and electrical package and a redesign of the roof drainage. Undisbursed loan and remaining equity no longer cover it. The loan is out of balance by about 600,000 dollars. The monitor also notes that the schedule has slipped five weeks.

The relationship manager turns to you and says: "So, what is going on?"

The question behind the question

The surface question is what happened. The real questions are three. Did you know before the monitor told us? Is the number going to get bigger? And will you fund the gap without a fight? If you answer the surface question with a long story, you have answered the real questions badly: you look surprised, you look unsure where the number ends, and you look like you are building a case for not paying.

The lines to say

Start with the bottom line. "Our own forecast shows the same overrun, within 50,000 dollars of the monitor's figure. We saw the mechanical and electrical buyout three weeks ago. We will cure the out-of-balance amount by depositing 600,000 dollars before the next draw, and I will confirm the date by Friday."

Then the cause, briefly. "Two drivers. The mechanical and electrical package bought out above its allowance because of equipment lead times, and the roof drainage redesign came from a coordination gap we found at the shop drawing stage. Here is the line-by-line reconciliation."

Then the containment. "We have priced the remaining packages. The two at risk are the elevators and the façade sealants, and here is our range for each. We have frozen discretionary changes, and every change above a stated amount now needs my written approval."

Then the schedule, honestly. "The five-week slip is real. Three weeks are recoverable through resequencing, which the contractor has priced; two are not, and we have added the interest cost for those weeks to the forecast."

Say that out loud now.

We saw it, here is the number, here is the deposit, here is how we stop it growing.

The lines never to say

Never say "the monitor is being conservative" unless you can prove it line by line, and even then say it as a reconciliation, not an accusation. Never say "the contractor will absorb it" unless you have it in writing. Never say "we can find it in contingency" when the monitor has already counted the contingency. Never offer a number for the remaining risk you have not built. Never say "this is standard" about an overrun; to a lender, standard overruns are what guarantees are for. And never ask in this meeting to reduce retainage or release the deferred part of your developer fee. That request, today, reads as a borrower short of cash.

When to stay silent

After you give the deposit commitment, stop talking. Let the risk officer ask the next question. Silence after a firm commitment signals that you have finished, not that you are hiding. The second moment for silence is when the monitor answers a question the lender put to it. Do not interrupt to correct. Note the point and raise it once, at the end, with evidence.

Holding your state

You will feel the heat. The useful move is reappraisal: name the sensation as readiness rather than threat, which is a habit supported by research on stress reappraisal. Slow your speaking pace and lower the pitch of the first sentence. Keep your hands still and your documents in order. If you have prepared, you have something solid to stand on, and the room will feel it. Breathing drills are for before the meeting, when you are parked, not on the drive in.

A worked example of the follow-up

Within 24 hours, send a one-page memo. Bottom line first: out of balance by about 600,000 dollars; deposit of 600,000 dollars by a stated date. Then a three-row table: mechanical and electrical overrun 700,000 dollars; roof drainage redesign 250,000 dollars; added interest for two unrecoverable weeks 150,000 dollars, totalling 1,100,000 dollars of new cost, less contingency already released of 500,000 dollars, equals 600,000 dollars. All figures hypothetical. Then the at-risk packages with ranges, and the change approval rule. One page, numbers reconciled to the monitor.

What the risk officer writes after you leave

After the meeting, the construction risk officer writes an internal note. I have written many. It answers four questions, and you have just given me the answers or failed to. Does the borrower have control of costs? Is the overrun contained, or still moving? Is the cure funded from a source we can verify? Should we tighten anything, such as the frequency of monitoring, a hold on the deferred developer fee, or a request for additional guarantor liquidity? A borrower who arrived with a matching forecast and a dated deposit gets a note that says contained, cured, no action. A borrower who argued gets "monitor closely", and that phrase follows the loan for the rest of its life, into every waiver request you make. You are, in effect, drafting my note with your answers.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is arriving surprised. If the monitor tells you about your own overrun, the lender concludes that you are not running the job. The control is your own monthly cost-to-complete forecast, finished before the draw meeting, so that the monitor confirms your number instead of revealing it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner argues the monitor's number in the room to avoid committing to a deposit. The lender hears a borrower who will not fund. Commit to curing the gap, then reconcile the number in writing afterward.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile-question pattern: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and the discipline of "I'll confirm by Friday." This meeting is that drill with money on the table. Acknowledge the overrun, bridge to the controls, answer with the deposit, and confirm the one thing you cannot confirm today by a stated date.

Recap

The lender's real questions are whether you knew, whether the number will grow and whether you will fund. Lead with the bottom line and the deposit, explain the cause briefly, show containment and an honest schedule, avoid the lines that sound like a cash-short borrower, use silence after commitments, and follow up in writing within a day.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap for the week, with Cole in the Auditor's Chair.
checklist: I finish my own cost-to-complete forecast before every draw meeting.
I open with the bottom line and the cure.
I explain causes briefly and reconcile them to the monitor.
I show the remaining at-risk packages with ranges I have built.
I never ask for retainage or fee releases in an overrun meeting.
I stay silent after a firm commitment.
I send a one-page follow-up within 24 hours.
head: Field checklist
speak: When the monitor reports an overrun, the lender is really asking three things: did I know, will the number grow, and will I fund it without a fight. So I lead with the bottom line. Our own forecast matches the monitor within a small margin; we saw the mechanical buyout weeks ago; we will deposit the shortfall before the next draw, and I will confirm the date by Friday. Then the causes, briefly, reconciled line by line. Then containment: the remaining packages at risk with ranges, a freeze on discretionary changes, and a written approval rule. Then the schedule, honestly. I never call the monitor conservative without proof, never promise the contractor will absorb it, and never ask for retainage or fee releases that day. After the commitment, I stop talking. Within 24 hours I send a one-page memo with the numbers reconciled.
terms: Relationship manager — the lender's officer who owns the borrower relationship and carries requests for waivers and consents internally.
Deferred developer fee — the part of a developer fee the lender requires to be paid only at or after completion.
Change approval threshold — the value above which a change order needs the owner's written approval before work proceeds.

hostile.q: Last month you told us the budget was fine. Why should we believe your forecast now?
hostile.a: Because last month the mechanical package was not bought out, and now it is; the forecast changed when the facts did, and I told you within three weeks. You can test my forecast against your monitor's every month, line by line. If you want more comfort, I will move to two-weekly cost reporting until completion and give your monitor access to our buyout log.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 40 Review: Draws, Reserves, Balance and Guarantees
summary: Six questions test the week's core ideas: draws, the lender's monitor, the in-balance test, the interest reserve, guarantees and carve-outs. Cole takes the Auditor's Chair to read a hypothetical draw certificate as a hostile auditor would. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: the lender funds a finished building one verified slice at a time, and when the money left will not finish it, someone with a guarantee closes the gap.

Recall

Q. What should you do immediately after making a firm commitment in a tense lender meeting?

A. Stop talking. Silence after a commitment signals that you have finished, and lets the lender ask the next question.

Q. What is an intercreditor agreement?

A. An agreement between lenders at different levels of the capital stack, for example senior and mezzanine, setting priority of payment, rights to cure defaults and limits on enforcement.

Q. What is a zoning envelope?

A. The three-dimensional limits zoning places on a site, including height, setbacks, coverage and density, which bound what can be built before any design begins.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, construction lending is where your plans meet someone else's discipline every month. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can sit with a construction lender as an equal. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is in a typical draw package, and who checks it?

Answer: The contractor's payment application, soft-cost invoices, an updated budget, lien waivers, a title update and a borrower's certificate. The lender's monitor checks work in place against the application, and the lender checks the documents and title.

Question 2. State the in-balance test.

Answer: Undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the cost to complete, including interest and soft costs. If not, the borrower deposits the shortfall before the next draw.

Question 3. Why is cost to complete not the same as budget remaining?

Answer: Budget remaining is the plan less spending. Cost to complete is a forecast of what finishing will actually take. When a project goes wrong, the two separate, and the in-balance test is built to catch that.

Question 4. How do you size an interest reserve?

Answer: Model interest on the draw curve during construction, at close to full balance during lease-up less any rent, gross it up because the reserve is borrowed, add a cushion for delay and rate, and re-run it whenever the schedule or rate moves.

Question 5. Name the four main construction guarantees.

Answer: Completion, cost overrun, carry until stabilisation, and repayment of principal, each with its own trigger, cap and burn-off.

Question 6. What is the difference between a loss carve-out and springing recourse?

Answer: A loss carve-out makes the guarantor liable for the lender's actual loss from a defined act. Springing recourse makes the guarantor liable for the whole loan on defined events, such as a voluntary bankruptcy filing or an unauthorised transfer.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Priya framed the loan as a series of draws, each released against verified work and a balanced loan. Ford and Roman took a composite case in which draws followed billing, the contractor failed and the guarantees were called, giving Rule 40. Priya priced the interest reserve and the guarantees. LEX taught how guarantees and carve-outs are read. Priya split an out-of-balance notice into overrun, delay and rate. Roman ran the draw meeting.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 40 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical borrower's draw certificate as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Draw Certificate No. 9. The Borrower certifies that: (a) all representations in the Loan Agreement remain true in all material respects; (b) the Loan is In Balance, the Budget remaining being 8,200,000 dollars against undisbursed Loan of 8,000,000 dollars and contingency of 400,000 dollars; (c) all amounts paid under prior draws have been paid to the parties entitled to them, save for amounts in dispute with the Contractor; (d) no Event of Default has occurred to the Borrower's knowledge; (e) the Contractor's application for 1,350,000 dollars reflects work in place. Signed: Project Coordinator.

The defects. First, clause (b) tests balance against budget remaining, not cost to complete, and adds contingency as if it were a source of funds, when contingency is part of the cost. Second, even on its own numbers, 8,200,000 dollars needed against 8,000,000 dollars available is out of balance; counting contingency as cash hides a gap. Third, clause (c) admits that prior draw money has not reached everyone entitled to it, which is exactly the condition that breeds liens, and it does not quantify the disputed amounts. Fourth, clause (d) is qualified by knowledge without saying whose knowledge or what inquiry was made. Fifth, clause (e) restates the contractor's claim without reference to the monitor's verification. Sixth, it is signed by a project coordinator; an auditor asks whether that person holds signing authority under the company's resolutions, and whether a false certificate by an unauthorised person still binds the borrower.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence behind each clause, and that list is your real lesson. For (a), the list of representations and the date each was last checked. For (b), the monitor's cost-to-complete report for the same date. For (c), the schedule of disputed amounts and the lien search. For (d), the names of the officers whose knowledge is meant and what they reviewed. For (e), the monitor's site report. For the signature, the board resolution naming who may sign. A certificate that cannot produce its evidence in an hour is a certificate signed on hope.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "What does the bank actually need from us during construction?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "The bank funds the building in monthly draws. Each draw needs evidence that the work is in place, which the bank's monitor checks, and proof that title is clean and subcontractors are being paid. Every month the bank also tests balance: the undisbursed loan plus any equity still to come must cover the full cost to complete. If it does not, we deposit the gap before the next draw. Interest is paid from a reserve inside the loan, so delay is expensive, because the loan is almost fully drawn by then. Behind all of it are guarantees: completion, cost overrun, carry and sometimes repayment, plus carve-outs that switch on personal recourse for bad acts. Our job is to keep our own cost-to-complete forecast, reconcile it to the monitor every month, size the reserve with a cushion, and negotiate caps and burn-offs on every guarantee. Then the bank confirms our numbers instead of discovering them."

Score your own answer before comparing. Did you open with the bottom line in one sentence? Did you state the in-balance test exactly, with cost to complete rather than budget? Did you name at least three guarantees and one way to limit them? Did you finish inside two minutes? If you missed any, record it again tomorrow. Kema's rule for this drill: the second recording is usually better, and the improvement is the point.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is signing documents, certificates and guarantees, that convert a project problem into a personal one without reading them. The control is a rule: nothing with your signature goes out until you can explain every number and every trigger in it.

The beginner's mistake

Memorising the four guarantees without asking what triggers each, what caps it and when it ends. The names are easy. The triggers decide your exposure.

Callback

In Week 35, Omar and LEX taught minute books, resolutions and signing authority as dull but load-bearing. The Auditor's Chair showed why: a draw certificate signed by someone without authority is a governance failure and a credit event at the same time.

Recap

Draws release money against verified work. The in-balance test compares available funds with cost to complete. The interest reserve is borrowed and sensitive to delay and rate. Guarantees and carve-outs decide personal exposure. Rule 40 keeps draws behind verified work and balance on an independent forecast.

head: The six questions
speak: Construction lending runs on draws. Each draw is released against evidence that the work is in place, checked by the lender's monitor, with clean title and subcontractors being paid. Every month the loan must stay in balance: undisbursed loan plus any equity still to come must cover the full cost to complete, or I deposit the gap before the next draw. Cost to complete is a forecast, not budget remaining, and contingency is part of the cost, not a source of funds. Interest is paid from a borrowed reserve, so delay and rate rises drain it fast. Behind the loan sit four guarantees, completion, cost overrun, carry and repayment, plus carve-outs that switch on personal recourse for bad acts. Rule 40: never let a draw run ahead of verified work in place, and certify balance only on an independent cost to complete. And nothing with my signature goes out until I can explain every number in it.
terms: Draw certificate — the borrower's signed statement, delivered with each draw, confirming representations, balance and payments.
Knowledge qualifier — wording that limits a statement to what a person knows, which needs to say whose knowledge and after what inquiry.
Signing authority — the power, granted by the company's resolutions, for a named person to bind it.

hostile.q: Your certificate says the loan is in balance, but it counts contingency as a source of funds. Is this certificate false?
hostile.a: On that basis it is wrong, and I will withdraw and replace it today. Contingency is part of cost to complete, not cash. The corrected certificate will test balance on the monitor's cost to complete against undisbursed loan and equity, quantify any disputed payments, be signed by an authorised officer, and if it shows a shortfall, it will come with the deposit.
